title: Fractures: Neurovascular Checks First
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: After a fracture or immobilization, repeated distal neurovascular assessment is essential. New severe pain, paresthesia, pallor, weakness, coolness, or worsening swelling can signal limb-threatening compromise and requires immediate escalation.
recognize: Pain, swelling, deformity, bruising, loss of function, and crepitus may occur with fracture.
Distal circulation, sensation, and movement must be compared with baseline and the opposite limb when appropriate.
priorities: Immobilize the injured area and avoid unnecessary manipulation.
Assess distal pulse, capillary refill, color, temperature, sensation, movement, and pain before and after splinting/casting or traction changes.
Escalate any new neurovascular deficit immediately.
assessMonitor: Trend pain quality and analgesic response rather than documenting pain score alone.
Inspect exposed skin and cast edges for pressure, drainage, odor, and swelling.
interventions: Elevate when ordered and appropriate to reduce swelling.
Use cold therapy during the early injury period when prescribed and protect skin from direct ice exposure.
Keep casts dry and intact; never insert objects under a cast.
medicationSafety: Assess sedation, respiratory status, and fall risk with opioid analgesics.
Report pain that is escalating despite analgesia because it can represent compartment syndrome rather than inadequate medication.
redFlags: Pain out of proportion or pain with passive stretch
Sudden dyspnea, hypoxemia, confusion, or petechiae after long-bone fracture
teaching: Report increasing tightness, numbness, color change, drainage, foul odor, fever, or inability to move digits.
delegationScope: Routine comfort measures may be delegated for a stable patient, but new pain or neurovascular changes require licensed-nurse assessment.
Do not delegate interpretation of neurovascular deterioration.
examTrap: Waiting for an absent pulse before recognizing compartment syndrome; pulselessness is a late finding.
oneLinePearl: After a fracture, trend the limb—not just the pain score.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons patient and clinical guidance

title: Compartment Syndrome: Limb Emergency
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: Acute compartment syndrome is a surgical emergency. Pain out of proportion, pain with passive stretch, tense swelling, paresthesia, or new weakness after fracture, crush injury, tight dressing, or reperfusion requires immediate escalation before permanent ischemic damage develops.
recognize: Severe escalating pain despite analgesia is an early clue.
Paresthesia and weakness suggest nerve ischemia; pallor and pulselessness are late.
priorities: Notify the RN/provider or activate urgent escalation immediately.
Maintain the extremity near heart level unless directed otherwise; excessive elevation can further reduce arterial perfusion.
Prepare for urgent pressure measurement and fasciotomy if ordered.
assessMonitor: Repeat pain, passive-stretch pain, sensation, motor function, skin temperature, color, capillary refill, and pulses.
Check whether a cast, splint, or dressing may be constrictive and follow orders/policy for relieving external pressure.
interventions: Keep the patient NPO if urgent surgery is likely per orders.
Do not delay escalation to complete routine documentation or administer repeated analgesics.
medicationSafety: Analgesia is appropriate but must not substitute for evaluation of unexplained escalating pain.
teaching: After discharge with a cast or splint, seek urgent care for rapidly worsening pain, numbness, weakness, or a cold/pale limb.
delegationScope: New neurovascular symptoms require licensed-nurse assessment and immediate escalation.
examTrap: Elevating the limb far above the heart or repeatedly medicating severe pain instead of treating the condition as an emergency.
oneLinePearl: Pain out of proportion + passive-stretch pain = compartment syndrome until proven otherwise.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons guidance

title: Hip Replacement: Protect the Joint and Prevent Clots
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
Physiological Integrity: Basic Care and Comfort
bottomLine: Post-hip-replacement care centers on safe mobility, dislocation precautions specific to the surgical approach, VTE prevention, pain control, and early recognition of infection or neurovascular compromise.
recognize: New severe hip pain, shortening, abnormal rotation, or inability to move the leg may indicate dislocation.
Unilateral calf swelling or pain and sudden dyspnea raise concern for VTE.
priorities: Use ordered positioning and approach-specific hip precautions.
Assist early mobilization with prescribed devices.
Apply ordered mechanical or pharmacologic VTE prophylaxis and reinforce adherence.
assessMonitor: Monitor wound, temperature, pain pattern, distal neurovascular status, mobility tolerance, and signs of DVT/PE.
Assess orthostatic symptoms and sedation before ambulation.
interventions: Use elevated seating/toileting devices if ordered.
Avoid prohibited hip positions according to the specific surgical approach rather than applying one universal rule.
medicationSafety: Coordinate analgesia so mobility can occur safely without excessive sedation.
redFlags: Sudden severe hip pain with deformity
Rapid wound drainage or spreading erythema
teaching: Use the prescribed walker or cane correctly, follow approach-specific movement restrictions, and report VTE or infection symptoms promptly.
delegationScope: Routine ambulation assistance may be delegated after the mobility plan is established; new pain, instability, or symptoms require licensed-nurse reassessment.
examTrap: Teaching the same hip precautions to every patient without considering the surgical approach and surgeon protocol.
oneLinePearl: Move early, prevent clots, and follow the actual surgical approach precautions.
sourceBasis: American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons hip replacement guidance

title: Osteoporosis and Fragility Fracture Prevention
bottomLine: Osteoporosis may be silent until a fragility fracture occurs. PN priorities are medication adherence and safety, adequate calcium/vitamin D intake as prescribed, weight-bearing activity, fall prevention, and reporting new back or hip pain promptly.
recognize: Low-trauma fracture, height loss, kyphosis, glucocorticoid exposure, low body weight, smoking, and advanced age increase concern.
Vertebral compression fractures may present as new back pain or progressive height loss.
priorities: Reduce fall hazards and support safe mobility.
Reinforce prescribed osteoporosis therapy and administration instructions.
Promote nutrition and activity within the patient's functional limits.
assessMonitor: Assess falls, gait, vision, orthostasis, medication burden, nutrition, pain, and adherence.
interventions: Encourage weight-bearing and resistance exercise when safe.
Support home safety measures and use of assistive devices.
medicationSafety: Oral bisphosphonates generally require administration with plain water on an empty stomach and remaining upright afterward; follow product-specific instructions.
Report jaw problems, severe esophageal symptoms, or new thigh/groin pain with antiresorptive therapy.
redFlags: New inability to bear weight after a fall
Acute severe back pain after minor trauma
teaching: Fall prevention matters as much as bone-density treatment because most serious osteoporotic injuries follow a fall.
delegationScope: Routine exercise assistance may be delegated after a safe plan is established; new pain or falls require assessment.
examTrap: Focusing only on calcium supplements while ignoring falls, medication technique, smoking, activity, and fracture history.
oneLinePearl: Protect the bone and prevent the fall.
sourceBasis: Bone Health and Osteoporosis Foundation clinical guidance

title: Burns: Airway, Perfusion, Then Wound
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: In major burns, airway and circulation outrank the appearance of the wound. Suspected inhalation injury, electrical burns, circumferential burns, large surface-area burns, or burns involving critical areas require rapid escalation and often burn-center consultation.
recognize: Facial burns, soot, singed nasal hair, hoarseness, carbonaceous sputum, stridor, or enclosed-space exposure suggest inhalation injury.
Electrical burns may cause deep internal injury despite limited skin findings.
priorities: Stop the burning process and assess airway, breathing, circulation, and exposure.
Remove constricting jewelry/clothing when safe before edema progresses.
Cover with clean dry material and prevent hypothermia; do not apply ice to major burns.
assessMonitor: Trend respiratory status, perfusion, mental status, urine output when ordered, pain, distal circulation with circumferential burns, and wound changes.
interventions: Use ordered fluid resuscitation for major burns and monitor response.
Provide wound care using prescribed clean/sterile technique and infection-prevention measures.
medicationSafety: IV analgesia may be needed in major burns; monitor respiratory status and hemodynamics.
Tetanus vaccination/TIG decisions depend on wound type and immunization history.
redFlags: Circumferential chest or limb burn with compromise
teaching: Avoid home remedies such as butter or direct ice on significant burns; seek urgent care for deep, electrical, chemical, inhalation, or extensive burns.
delegationScope: Major-burn assessment and deterioration require licensed-nurse evaluation; routine comfort and hygiene tasks may be delegated only when stable and appropriate.
examTrap: Treating the visible burn before recognizing a threatened airway.
oneLinePearl: Burn exam questions start with airway and perfusion, not dressing choice.

title: Dehiscence and Evisceration
clientNeeds: Physiological Integrity: Reduction of Risk Potential
bottomLine: A postoperative wound that separates requires immediate protection and escalation. If organs protrude, do not push them back; cover with sterile dressings moistened with sterile normal saline, reduce abdominal strain, and prepare for urgent surgical management.
recognize: A sudden gush of serosanguineous drainage can precede visible wound separation.
Evisceration is protrusion of abdominal contents through the incision.
priorities: Stay with the patient and call for immediate help.
Position to reduce abdominal tension, commonly supine with knees bent if tolerated.
Cover exposed viscera with sterile saline-moistened dressings and keep them moist.
assessMonitor: Monitor vital signs, pain, bleeding, wound appearance, and signs of shock or infection.
interventions: Keep NPO and prepare for urgent operative management as ordered.
Use abdominal splinting for coughing and movement after stabilization if appropriate.
medicationSafety: Administer prescribed analgesia and IV fluids while monitoring hemodynamic status.
teaching: Report sudden drainage, opening of the incision, fever, or increasing redness rather than waiting for the next visit.
delegationScope: Evisceration is not a task to delegate; the licensed nurse must assess, protect the wound, and escalate.
examTrap: Attempting to replace protruding organs into the abdomen.
oneLinePearl: Cover, flex, NPO, call—never push organs back in.
sourceBasis: AORN perioperative and surgical wound-care principles

title: Cellulitis: Watch for Spread and Sepsis
bottomLine: Cellulitis is a spreading skin and soft-tissue infection. Marking borders and trending systemic symptoms helps identify treatment failure; rapid progression, severe pain, crepitus, bullae, hypotension, or toxicity requires urgent evaluation for deeper infection or sepsis.
recognize: Typical findings include warmth, erythema, edema, and tenderness with poorly demarcated borders.
Purulence or abscess changes the management pathway and may require drainage.
priorities: Assess for systemic illness and rapidly progressive disease.
Administer antibiotics on schedule and monitor response.
Elevate an affected limb when appropriate and manage pain.
assessMonitor: Trend erythema borders, temperature, pain, swelling, drainage, vital signs, glucose in patients with diabetes, and adherence.
interventions: Use wound cultures when ordered for purulent or complicated infections; routine uncomplicated nonpurulent cellulitis may not require a culture.
Protect broken skin and reinforce hygiene.
medicationSafety: Confirm allergy history and monitor for antibiotic adverse effects.
Failure to improve can reflect resistant organisms, abscess, poor perfusion, nonadherence, or a noninfectious mimic.
teaching: Complete prescribed therapy and seek care for rapid spread, fever, worsening pain, or systemic symptoms.
delegationScope: Routine hygiene can be delegated for stable patients; worsening infection or systemic symptoms require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Assuming every red swollen leg is cellulitis without considering DVT, venous stasis, gout, or necrotizing infection.
oneLinePearl: Mark the border, trend the patient, and fear pain out of proportion.
sourceBasis: CDC skin infection and sepsis guidance
IDSA skin and soft-tissue infection guideline

title: C. difficile: Contact Precautions and Soap-and-Water Hygiene
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: New significant diarrhea during or after antibiotic exposure raises concern for C. difficile. Use contact precautions, soap-and-water handwashing when caring for a patient with C. difficile, dedicated equipment, and sporicidal environmental cleaning per policy.
recognize: Risk rises with recent antibiotics, healthcare exposure, advanced age, and severe illness.
Testing formed stool or asymptomatic patients can produce misleading results because colonization is possible.
priorities: Initiate appropriate isolation promptly when suspected per facility policy.
Monitor hydration, electrolytes, stool frequency, abdominal pain/distention, and systemic illness.
Administer prescribed therapy and stop unnecessary inciting antibiotics when directed.
assessMonitor: Trend stool frequency, intake/output, creatinine/electrolytes when ordered, abdominal findings, fever, WBC trends when available, and hemodynamics.
interventions: Use gown and gloves for room entry/contact per policy.
Clean reusable equipment and the environment with products effective against spores.
medicationSafety: Avoid antidiarrheal drugs unless specifically ordered because slowing intestinal motility may be unsafe in severe colitis.
redFlags: High fever or severe systemic toxicity
teaching: Wash hands with soap and water after toileting and before eating; alcohol hand rub alone is less reliable against spores.
delegationScope: Isolation and hygiene tasks may be shared with trained staff, but dehydration, worsening abdominal findings, or systemic illness require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Relying on alcohol hand sanitizer alone after caring for a patient with C. difficile.
oneLinePearl: C. diff means contact precautions, soap and water, and spores on the environment.
sourceBasis: CDC C. difficile infection prevention guidance

title: Herpes Zoster: Painful Dermatomal Rash
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Shingles usually causes a painful unilateral dermatomal vesicular eruption. Eye or ear involvement, disseminated disease, severe immunocompromise, or neurologic symptoms require urgent escalation; infection-control precautions depend on localization and immune status.
recognize: Burning, tingling, or pain may precede grouped vesicles in a dermatome.
Lesions that cross multiple dermatomes or are widespread suggest disseminated disease.
priorities: Cover lesions when possible and follow transmission precautions appropriate to localized versus disseminated disease and immune status.
Administer antiviral therapy promptly when prescribed.
Escalate facial lesions near the eye or ear.
assessMonitor: Assess pain, lesion distribution, vision/eye symptoms, facial weakness, hearing changes, immune status, and signs of secondary bacterial infection.
interventions: Use cool compresses and prescribed pain measures.
Avoid contact between active lesions and susceptible high-risk individuals until lesions crust.
medicationSafety: Renal dosing may be required for acyclovir/valacyclovir; maintain hydration as appropriate.
redFlags: Vesicles on the tip of the nose with ocular symptoms
teaching: Vaccination reduces future shingles risk but is not a treatment for an active episode; follow current CDC recommendations.
delegationScope: Routine skin care may be delegated when stable; eye/ear/neurologic symptoms require licensed-nurse assessment.
examTrap: Treating facial shingles near the eye as routine skin disease.
oneLinePearl: Dermatomal vesicles are shingles; eye, ear, or widespread disease changes the urgency.
sourceBasis: CDC shingles clinical and vaccination guidance

title: Tetanus Prevention After a Wound
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Tetanus prevention after injury depends on both wound type and vaccination history. Clean the wound, remove foreign or necrotic material, determine whether a tetanus-containing vaccine is due, and determine whether TIG is indicated for dirty/major wounds with inadequate immunity.
recognize: Dirty/major wounds include punctures, contaminated wounds, bites, burns, crush injuries, compound fractures, frostbite, and wounds with devitalized tissue.
Antibiotics are not used solely to prevent tetanus.
priorities: Clean and assess the wound.
Verify primary-series completion and timing of the last tetanus-containing vaccine.
Administer vaccine and/or TIG when indicated according to CDC guidance and orders.
assessMonitor: Assess wound contamination, devitalized tissue, immunization record, severe immunodeficiency/HIV status, and infection signs.
interventions: Remove foreign material and support debridement as ordered.
Document vaccine/TIG administration and provide follow-up instructions.
medicationSafety: TIG provides temporary passive protection and is never indicated for clean minor wounds.
Do not substitute prophylactic antibiotics for vaccine/TIG decisions.
teaching: Keep routine tetanus immunization current and seek wound evaluation when vaccination history is uncertain or the wound is dirty/major.
delegationScope: The licensed nurse verifies immunization history, assesses wound risk, and administers ordered prophylaxis within scope/policy.
examTrap: Giving antibiotics as tetanus prophylaxis or assuming every wound needs TIG.
oneLinePearl: Wound type + vaccine history decide tetanus prophylaxis.
sourceBasis: CDC Clinical Guidance for Wound Management to Prevent Tetanus
